newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE - Men without fingers guard Mother Teresa's clinic.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Men without fingers guard Mother Teresa's clinic.

text.p: Men who have lost their fingers guard the gates at Mother Teresa's sprawling leprosy clinic on the outskirts of India's eastern city of Calcutta.
"Here we allocate jobs to each of the patients according to their deformity," said Brother Vinod, who supervises the clinic at Titagarh, 25 km (15 miles) north of Calcutta.
More than 300 ill and deformed leprosy victims, rejected by their families and reduced to begging in Calcutta's grimy streets, have found a home, jobs and a new life at the clinic.
Brother Vinod said nearly 38,000 patients have been treated at the clinic since it was first set up on the site of an old leprosy sanatorium in the late 1950s.

Mother Teresa's religious order, the Missionaries of Charity, runs 462 similar clinics all over India. They are one facet of the ailing nun's work with the poor, the sick and the dying that has won her the sobriquet "Saint of the Gutters".
Mother Teresa, 86, has been fighting hard to throw off a respiratory problem that delayed her recovery from life-saving heart surgery last month.

About 475 men and women who have acute leprosy are being treated in the wards of the long, low building at Titagarh. It may take one or two years of therapy before they are cured, and even then some will be left with crippling disfigurements, Vinod said.
HIGH DROP-OUT RATE
"But the drop-out rate is very high. We have about 1,700 to 1,800 in regular treatment at any given time. The rest lose interest within two or three months," he added.
Leprosy begins with spots and thickening of the skin, and gradually attacks the nerves. Left untreated, it eats away the tissues of the extremities and victims may lose their limbs.
"Most of them come to us as beggars, and after we treat them they have nothing to do but go back to begging," Vinod said.
To avoid this, the clinic teaches them simple trades.

Fifty wooden looms clacked rhythmically in the clinic's weaving section. Men and women systematically worked the foot pedals, simultaneously moving the frames to weave horizontal and vertical threads.
Women turned spinning-wheels on the floor to make thread.
"I came here with lesions on my face and hands," said Zarina Bibi, 30, as she wove a bedsheet. "They gave me some medicine that puffed me up to a huge size before I got better."
Zarina said she has spent four years at the leprosy centre. It was a year and a half before she was completely cured.
Long before then, her husband deserted her, taking the couple's 15-year-old son with him. Zarina and her 10-year-old daughter struggled alone before she came to the clinic.
"I am able to weave four or five bedsheets or sarees every day," she said. "That gives me some money."
DAILY EARNINGS
Rehabilitated patients who weave at the clinic earn about 20 rupees (55 U.S. cents) for each completed piece, Vinod said. Typically, each worker completes two or three pieces every day.
"All the sarees for the Missionaries of Charity -- some 7,000 pieces to be used all over the world -- are made here," he said.
The Missionaries of Charity wear a simple white saree with a distinctive edge of three blue stripes.
The leprosy patients greeted visitors with folded hands and a "namaste", the traditional Indian greeting.
In the physiotherapy section, Vikram Paswan, 20, grimaced as hot wax was poured over his contracted hands to help straighten out his fingers.
"It hurts now," the attendant said, watching the wax cool to form a thick skin. "But it will soon straighten them out."
Across the passage, a 30-year-old woman sat on a bench, moaning as a nurse poured hydrogen peroxide over her right foot, in which the disease had gnawed out a dirty ragged crescent below the toes.
The nurse used a tweezer to pick maggots out of the lesion one by one. "Stop making a noise now," she said sternly. "What were you doing when the disease was eating up your foot?"
